debates.comment: Correcting an internal contradiction regarding martyrdom traditions is a genuine factual and editorial improvement.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Philip the Apostle

debates.before: under the Emperor Domitian
debates.after: possibly under the Emperor Domitian
debates.concern: The tradition that Philip preached and was martyred at Hierapolis is longstanding, but assigning the event specifically to the reign of Domitian is not established with the same confidence. The qualification should make clear that this is a later traditional chronology.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the attribution to Domitian or verify it against a reliable historical source.
debates.comment: Adding the qualifier correctly reflects the uncertainty in dating ancient martyrdom traditions.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Matthias

debates.before: one of the wider circle of seventy-two disciples Jesus had sent out ahead of him
debates.after: Some later traditions identify him as one of the seventy-two disciples Jesus had sent out ahead of him
debates.concern: Acts identifies Matthias as someone who accompanied Jesus from the baptism of John until the Ascension, but it does not identify him as one of the seventy-two. That identification should be presented as a later tradition rather than as established fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the identification as a later tradition, as in the proposed replacement.
debates.comment: Important distinction to frame pious tradition correctly rather than present it as scriptural fact.

debates.before: or, in the account preserved by Dorotheus, to the interior of a remote and hostile land near the port of Hyssus, where he is remembered as preaching among fierce and unwelcoming peoples
debates.after: or, in an account attributed to Dorotheus, to a remote region where he is remembered as preaching among hostile peoples
debates.concern: The detailed geographical description and attribution to Dorotheus are sufficiently specific to require verification, and traditions about Matthias's mission locations vary substantially. The passage should avoid presenting a potentially conflated account as a secure description.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the Dorotheus attribution and the identification of Hyssus; if they cannot be firmly established, use the more cautious wording proposed.
debates.comment: Softening the specific geographical details appropriately reflects the uncertain nature of early traditions.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Martha, Mary & Lazarus
Proofread articles — Sts. Timothy & Titus

debates.before: the only one of Paul's close companions the tradition remembers as dying peacefully
debates.after: and tradition remembers Titus as having died peacefully
debates.concern: The exclusivity claim is not established by the passage and risks presenting an incomplete tradition as a definitive comparison of the deaths of Paul's companions. Titus's peaceful death is itself traditional and should be stated without the unsupported 'only one' claim.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported exclusivity claim and identify Titus's peaceful death as a tradition.
debates.comment: The exclusivity claim in the original ('the only one') introduces a comparative historical claim about traditions of all Paul's companions that is hard to verify; dropping it makes the text more reliable.

tasks.description: Record audio narration — St. Bartholomew
Record audio narration — St. Paul
Record audio narration — St. Peter
Record audio narration — St. Jude Thaddeus
Record audio narration — St. James the Less
Record audio narration — St. Barnabas
Record audio narration — St. Mary Magdalene
Record audio narration — Blessed Virgin Mary
Record audio narration — St. James the Greater
Record audio narration — St. Stephen
Record audio narration — St. Veronica
Record audio narration — St. Joseph
Record audio narration — Sts. Anne & Joachim
Record audio narration — St. Raphael the Archangel
Record audio narration — St. Michael the Archangel
Proofread articles — St. Ignatius of Antioch

debates.before: Ignatius is the first writer to insist clearly on the threefold ministry of a single bishop with his priests and deacons as the guarantee of unity
debates.after: Ignatius is among the earliest surviving writers to describe clearly the threefold ministry of bishop, priests, and deacons as essential to the Church's unity
debates.concern: The absolute claim that Ignatius was the first writer to insist on this ministry is difficult to establish, and the wording can suggest that he originated or definitively settled the structure rather than being its earliest clear surviving witness.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use qualified wording identifying Ignatius as an early surviving witness rather than asserting priority absolutely.
debates.comment: The revision avoids an absolute priority claim while accurately capturing Ignatius's historical significance.

debates.before: uses, for the first time in surviving Christian literature, the phrase that would name the Church forever after — the Catholic Church
debates.after: uses one of the earliest surviving instances of the expression "the Catholic Church"
debates.concern: The priority claim is too absolute without specifying the corpus and surviving evidence, while "would name the Church forever after" is rhetorically sweeping. Ignatius provides the earliest surviving use commonly cited, but the wording should not imply that this single passage established the Church's name in a simple, exhaustive sense.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the historical priority claim and remove the sweeping causal formulation.
debates.comment: The revised phrasing avoids rhetorically sweeping language while maintaining historical accuracy.

debates.section: A Voice from the Sub-Apostolic Age
debates.before: already naming itself Catholic — not a later structure imposed on a formless beginning, but the visible shape of the faith from the first. For this reason his seven epistles have been cited in every age as evidence
debates.after: already using the term Catholic and displaying an ordered, sacramental ecclesial life—not a structure that first appeared only in a later period. His seven epistles have therefore long been used as important evidence
debates.concern: The contrast with a "formless beginning" imputes a disputed historiographical position to other accounts, and "cited in every age" is an unsupported universal claim. The historical point can be made without overstating the evidence or framing the issue polemically.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the sweeping and adversarial formulation with a measured description of what the letters show and how they are used by historians.
debates.comment: The revision removes polemical phrasing and unsupported universal claims while keeping the core historical point.

debates.before: With Clement of Rome and Polycarp he is numbered among the Apostolic Fathers, the men who received the faith directly from the Apostles and handed it on.
debates.after: With Clement of Rome and Polycarp he is numbered among the Apostolic Fathers, early Christian writers associated with the generation that followed the Apostles and whose works witness to the faith they received and handed on.
debates.concern: The definition is too restrictive and potentially inaccurate: the Apostolic Fathers are not uniformly established as men who personally received the faith directly from the Apostles. The category generally refers to early post-apostolic Christian authors, some of whom had direct apostolic connections.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Define the Apostolic Fathers by their early post-apostolic setting and apostolic connections without asserting direct personal reception in every case.
debates.comment: The revision provides a more precise and academically sound definition of the Apostolic Fathers.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Polycarp
Proofread articles — St. Justin Martyr
Proofread articles — St. Irenaeus
Proofread articles — Sts. Perpetua & Felicity

debates.text: a decree of the Emperor Septimius Severus forbade conversion to Christianity under pain of death
debates.concern: The Severan policy and its precise legal scope are debated. The surviving evidence more securely supports an imperial prohibition on new conversions than a clearly documented general decree imposing death specifically for conversion.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the legal wording and scope, or qualify the sentence: "Around 203, amid an imperial policy forbidding new conversions to Christianity, catechumens in Carthage were arrested..."
debates.before: a decree of the Emperor Septimius Severus forbade conversion to Christianity under pain of death
debates.after: amid an imperial policy forbidding new conversions to Christianity
debates.comment: The revision avoids the specific, debated claim of a formal decree carrying the death penalty while retaining the historical context of persecution.

debates.text: She gave birth to a healthy daughter
debates.concern: The Passion records that Felicity gave birth to a daughter who was taken in by a Christian woman, but it does not establish that the child was healthy. This adds an unsupported medical detail.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove "healthy": "She gave birth to a daughter, entrusted at once to the care of a Christian sister..."
debates.before: She gave birth to a healthy daughter
debates.after: She gave birth to a daughter
debates.comment: Removing the unsupported adjective 'healthy' is a precise and worthwhile correction to the source text.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Pope St. Callistus I

debates.before: He was freed through the intercession of Pope St. Victor I, who arranged for his release along with other Christian prisoners
debates.after: He was eventually released from the mines, apparently through the intervention of Marcia, the influential woman who secured the release of several Christian prisoners
debates.concern: The surviving account of Callistus's release is polemical and differs from this attribution. Hippolytus associates Callistus's release with Marcia's intervention, while Victor is associated in some accounts with sending him to Sardinia. The present wording states Victor's role too confidently.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the precise account of Callistus's release and qualify the attribution if relying on Hippolytus's hostile narrative.
debates.comment: The attribution to Marcia from Hippolytus is the standard historical detail for his release, making the revision more accurate.

debates.section: A Quiet Reign, A Violent End
debates.before: Callistus was killed in a local riot around 222, thrown from a window into a well in Trastevere
debates.after: Callistus is traditionally said to have died around 222 after being thrown from a window into a well in Trastevere, although the details of the account are reported in later sources
debates.concern: The Depositio Martyrum supports Callistus's early veneration as a martyr, but the detailed account of a riot, a window, and a well comes from later and potentially unreliable narratives. It should not be presented as securely documented history.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Present the manner of death as a tradition or later account unless a reliable early source can substantiate these details.
debates.comment: Clarifying that the window and well story is a traditional account prevents presenting legend as hardened fact.

debates.section: A Quiet Reign, A Violent End
debates.before: a death the ancient Depositio Martirum of the fourth century remembered as true martyrdom
debates.after: a death commemorated as martyrdom in the fourth-century Depositio Martyrum
debates.concern: The Depositio Martyrum is an early list of commemorations and burials, but describing it as establishing a 'true martyrdom' overstates what the source itself demonstrates, especially when the circumstances of Callistus's death are uncertain. The title is also normally spelled Depositio Martyrum.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use more neutral wording about the fourth-century commemoration and avoid treating the calendar entry alone as proof of the historical circumstances.
debates.comment: Fixes the spelling of Depositio Martyrum and tightens the phrasing to better reflect the source.

debates.before: Callistus is remembered as the earliest pope listed as a genuine martyr in the Church's oldest surviving liturgical calendars
debates.after: Callistus is among the earliest popes commemorated as a martyr in the Church's surviving fourth-century Roman calendars
debates.concern: The claim that he was the earliest pope listed as a 'genuine martyr' is imprecise and potentially misleading. The relevant Depositio Martyrum is a fourth-century Roman commemorative list, not straightforwardly a liturgical calendar, and the source's commemoration does not by itself establish the modern historical qualification 'genuine.'
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the Depositio Martyrum accurately and describe Callistus as commemorated or venerated as a martyr rather than asserting that the calendar proves his status as a genuine martyr.
debates.comment: Removes the potentially confusing and subjective 'genuine martyr' phrasing in favor of a safer historical description.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Cecilia

debates.section: Three Days of Dying, and of Giving
debates.before: Her body, discovered incorrupt when her tomb was opened in 1599, was found lying on its side, hands folded in prayer
debates.after: When her tomb was opened in 1599, her body was reported to be remarkably well preserved and lying on its side, hands folded in prayer
debates.concern: The 1599 discovery and the body's exact condition and posture are reported in devotional and historical accounts, but presenting the body as definitively incorrupt states a contested tradition as established fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the report as a historical or devotional account rather than asserting incorruption as an independently established fact.
debates.comment: Reframing the incorruptibility claim from established fact to reported tradition is doctrinally and historically more careful.

debates.section: The Song That Has Never Ceased
debates.before: Since the founding of the Roman Academy of Music under her patronage in 1584
debates.after: Since the founding of the Roman Academy of Music under her patronage in 1585
debates.concern: The Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia is generally dated to 1585, not 1584. The date should be checked and corrected.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace 1584 with 1585 if the sentence refers to the founding of the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia.
debates.comment: 1585 is the standard founding date for the Academy.

debates.section: Three Days of Dying, and of Giving
debates.before: Roman law forbidding a fourth stroke, he left her to die slowly of her wounds
debates.after: according to the traditional account, he left her to die slowly of her wounds after striking three times
debates.concern: The three blows and the claim that Roman law prevented a fourth are details of the traditional Passion narrative, not securely documented historical facts. The wording currently presents the legal explanation too definitively.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Retain the episode only as part of the traditional account, or verify the specific claim about Roman legal practice.
debates.comment: Adding 'according to the traditional account' appropriately contextualizes a legendary detail of the martyrdom.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Pontian & Hippolytus

debates.before: the Church's first antipope
debates.after: often regarded as the Church's first antipope
debates.concern: Hippolytus is commonly described as the first antipope, but the designation is retrospective and depends on identifying him as a rival bishop of Rome during the disputed succession. The categorical wording should acknowledge that historical terminology.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the designation as customary or commonly regarded rather than presenting it as an entirely uncontested historical title.
debates.comment: Clarifies the retrospective nature of the title, which is historically accurate.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Pope St. Fabian

debates.before: requiring all subjects to sacrifice to the Roman gods on pain of death
debates.after: requiring inhabitants to sacrifice to the Roman gods under threat of severe penalties, which could include imprisonment, torture, or death
debates.concern: The Decian edict required sacrifice and certification, but refusal did not uniformly result in an automatic death sentence. Penalties varied, and the phrase 'on pain of death' overstates the edict's operation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe the sacrifice requirement and the range of penalties more cautiously rather than implying that every refusal was automatically punishable by death.
debates.comment: Adding nuance regarding the tiered penalties of the Decian persecution is historically more precise than an automatic death sentence.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Agatha
Proofread articles — Pope St. Cornelius

debates.before: helped bring roughly a hundred African bishops into agreement with Rome
debates.after: helped bring many African bishops into agreement with Rome
debates.concern: The precise number of African bishops involved is uncertain or may conflate different councils and correspondence. Cyprian's council at Carthage is commonly described as involving about seventy bishops, while later African support may have involved more. The wording should not present roughly one hundred as an established figure without a clear basis.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the intended number and its source, or replace the precise figure with a non-numerical description such as “helped bring many African bishops into agreement with Rome.”
debates.comment: The exact number is debated, so softening 'roughly a hundred' to 'many' avoids an unsupported specific figure.

debates.before: This compassionate but disciplined approach became the enduring model for how the Church would handle grave sin among the baptized for centuries afterward.
debates.after: This compassionate but disciplined approach helped shape the Church's developing practice of reconciling grave sinners among the baptized.
debates.concern: The claim that Cornelius's policy became the enduring model for the Church for centuries afterward is broad and presents a complex, gradually developing penitential practice as a direct and lasting consequence of this controversy.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the historical scope and avoid implying that later penitential practice was simply established by Cornelius's policy.
debates.comment: The revision avoids overstating a single pope's policy as the direct blueprint for centuries of subsequent penitential discipline.

debates.before: where, worn down by the hardships of banishment, he died in June 253
debates.after: where he died in June 253
debates.concern: The assertion that exile's hardships caused or materially contributed to Cornelius's death is not established by the wording supplied and may be an inferred circumstance rather than documented history.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported causal description unless a reliable source specifically documents Cornelius's condition and the cause of death.
debates.comment: Removing the causal link to banishment hardships eliminates an unnecessary and uncertain inference.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Lawrence
Proofread articles — St. Cyprian
Proofread articles — Pope St. Sixtus II & Companions

debates.before: along with four of his deacons — Januarius, Vincent, Magnus, and Stephen — who were beheaded together with him
debates.after: along with four of his deacons — Januarius, Vincent, Magnus, and Stephen — who were beheaded together with him; two other deacons, Felicissimus and Agapitus, were martyred shortly afterward
debates.concern: The sentence implies that these were the only deacons associated with Sixtus's martyrdom. The traditional account also names Felicissimus and Agapitus, who were executed shortly afterward.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Mention Felicissimus and Agapitus and distinguish their later martyrdom from the execution of Sixtus and the four deacons who were killed with him.
debates.comment: Provides important traditional historical completeness regarding the full group of deacons martyred with Sixtus.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Denis & Companions

debates.before: though the name in fact derives from an earlier Roman temple site
debates.after: though its exact etymology is debated, with a traditional derivation from the Latin Mons Martyrum ('mountain of martyrs') and an alternative connection to an earlier Roman temple site
debates.concern: The sentence presents the Roman-temple derivation as established fact, but the name Montmartre is traditionally derived from Mons Martyrum ('mountain of martyrs') and its etymology is debated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Present the Roman-temple derivation as an alternative theory rather than the established meaning of the name.
debates.comment: The revision correctly captures the nuance and scholarly debate regarding the etymology of Montmartre.

debates.section: A Devotion Confused with Another Dionysius
debates.before: He was identified with the Athenian convert of St. Paul mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.
debates.after: Denis was identified with the Athenian convert of St. Paul mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.
debates.concern: The pronoun 'He' is ambiguous because the preceding sentence introduces the first-century Dionysius the Areopagite, making it unclear whether the sentence refers to Denis or to the Areopagite. The sentence also repeats the identification already stated immediately before it.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Name Denis explicitly and remove the duplication, for example: 'Denis was consequently identified with the Athenian convert of St. Paul mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.'
debates.comment: Replacing the pronoun with the proper name resolves a genuine ambiguity in the text.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Tarcisius

debates.before: alongside his deacons Sixtus II and Companions
debates.after: alongside his deacons, who are commemorated with him as Sixtus II and Companions
debates.concern: The wording incorrectly lists Sixtus II as one of his own deacons, even though Sixtus II is the pope being described. The phrase appears to conflate the pope with the collective designation for him and his companions.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Clarify that Sixtus II and his deacons are commemorated together, rather than identifying Sixtus II as one of the deacons.
debates.comment: The original phrasing erroneously conflates the Pope with his deacons.

debates.before: Pope Sixtus II — who according to the same tradition governed Rome during these same years of persecution and would himself be martyred not long after, alongside his deacons Sixtus II and Companions
debates.after: Pope Sixtus II — who according to the same tradition governed Rome during these same years of persecution and would himself be martyred not long after, alongside his deacons and companions
debates.concern: The sentence awkwardly repeats 'Sixtus II' inside the same clause ('alongside his deacons Sixtus II and Companions'), which is internally contradictory and confusing since Sixtus II is the pope just named.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct the repetitive and contradictory wording regarding Sixtus II and his companions.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Cosmas & Damian

debates.text: That day was probably in the year 287
debates.concern: The traditional Acts do not establish a securely documented year for the brothers' martyrdom, and proposed dates vary. The wording appropriately signals uncertainty, but assigning 287 as the probable year requires supporting evidence and may be more precise than the historical record permits.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the proposed date against a reliable historical source, or revise to say that the date and year of their martyrdom are uncertain and traditionally associated with the persecution under Diocletian.
debates.before: That day was probably in the year 287
debates.after: The date and year of their martyrdom are uncertain, though tradition places it during the persecution under Diocletian
debates.comment: Acknowledging the uncertainty of the specific year is historically more accurate than asserting 287.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Sebastian

debates.section: A Secret Christian in the Guard
debates.before: came from Milan
debates.after: was born at Narbonne and raised in Milan
debates.concern: The traditional account generally places Sebastian's birth at Narbonne and describes him as having been raised or educated in Milan. Saying simply that he came from Milan misstates the traditional biography and makes Milan his place of origin.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the phrase with wording that distinguishes Sebastian's birthplace from his Milanese upbringing.
debates.comment: Adding Narbonne clarifies his traditional birthplace while retaining Milan as his home.

debates.before: Mauretanian archers
debates.after: Mauritanian archers
debates.concern: The conventional English spelling of the ancient North African region and its inhabitants is usually 'Mauritanian,' not 'Mauretanian.' If the intended claim is that the archers came from Mauretania, the terminology should be checked against the source.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the source's wording and use the standard English form 'Mauritanian' unless a historically specific alternative is intended.
debates.comment: Mauritanian is the more standard English spelling for the region.

debates.before: making Sebastian one of the more historically well-attested Roman martyrs
debates.after: providing early evidence for Sebastian's veneration in Rome
debates.concern: The Depositio Martyrum provides important early evidence for a Roman cult of Sebastian, but calling him one of the 'more historically well-attested Roman martyrs' is a broader comparative judgment than the evidence cited here establishes, especially since the article also acknowledges that the narrative details come from later legendary Acts.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Retain the specific claim about early Roman veneration and remove or substantiate the broader comparative assessment.
debates.comment: The revision is much more defensible given the legendary nature of the Acts of St. Sebastian.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Agnes

debates.section: A Constancy Tested to the End
debates.before: writing barely a lifetime after her death
debates.after: writing several decades after her death
debates.concern: St. Ambrose died around 397, while Agnes's traditional martyrdom is usually dated to around 304; his relevant testimony therefore comes roughly seven decades later, not barely a lifetime later.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the phrase with wording that accurately describes the interval between Agnes's death and Ambrose's writings.
debates.comment: Seven decades is better described as several decades rather than barely a lifetime.

debates.section: A Constancy Tested to the End
debates.before: still too young by Roman law to be legally condemned for most crimes
debates.after: still very young by Roman standards
debates.concern: The claim that Roman law generally made Agnes too young to be legally condemned for most crimes is an overly broad and potentially false legal assertion. Roman criminal law did not operate through a simple general exemption of this kind, and the article does not establish the relevant legal rule or charge.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the specific legal claim unless it is supported by a precise historical source; retain only a more cautious description of Agnes's youth.
debates.comment: Removes an overly complex and potentially inaccurate legal claim regarding Roman law.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Vincent of Saragossa

debates.text: composed in poetic form by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius within a generation of his death
debates.concern: Prudentius's poetic account dates from roughly a century after Vincent's death, not within a generation. Moreover, Prudentius's work is a poetic martyr hymn rather than straightforwardly an Acts narrative.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace this with wording such as: "According to traditional accounts of his martyrdom, poetically commemorated by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius about a century after his death,"
debates.before: composed in poetic form by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius within a generation of his death
debates.after: preserved in traditional accounts and poetically commemorated by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius about a century after his death
debates.comment: Prudentius wrote about a century after the martyrdom, making the correction factually important.

debates.text: Dacian, evidently regarding the eloquent young deacon as the more dangerous of the two
debates.concern: This attributes a specific motive and comparative assessment to Dacian without clear historical evidence. The traditional accounts may describe Vincent receiving harsher treatment, but they do not establish what Dacian privately regarded as the reason.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the inferred motive and state simply that, according to the traditional account, Dacian subjected Vincent to escalating and prolonged torture while Valerius was sentenced to exile.
debates.before: Dacian, evidently regarding the eloquent young deacon as the more dangerous of the two, subjected Vincent alone to escalating and prolonged torture
debates.after: Dacian then subjected Vincent alone to escalating and prolonged torture
debates.comment: Removing unwarranted speculation about Dacian's private motives improves historical precision.

debates.before: You may rest assured that you will tire of inflicting torments sooner than we of suffering them.
debates.after: You will tire of inflicting torments sooner than I of suffering them.
debates.concern: The quotation in the Quoted Sources block (and its matching prose paraphrase in 'Torments Endured') uses first-person plural ('we... suffering them'), but the traditional Acts of St. Vincent attribute this statement to him in the singular ('I' or 'he'). Furthermore, in the prose section 'Torments Endured', the text says 'they would tire of inflicting torment long before he tired of enduring it', creating an inconsistency between the prose and the quote block.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Update the quoted source text to match standard historical accounts of Prudentius's hymn/Acts where Vincent speaks in the singular.
debates.comment: The singular wording better matches the traditional attribution to St. Vincent and resolves the inconsistency with the accompanying prose.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Nereus & Achilleus

debates.before: an image of decisive rejection of violence for the sake of the Gospel
debates.after: an image of decisive rejection of military service for the sake of the Gospel
debates.concern: Damasus's account presents the saints as abandoning military service, but the sentence broadens this into a general rejection of violence. That interpretation may suggest a developed pacifist position not established by the epitaph itself.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Limit the interpretation to their renunciation of military service, unless a source specifically supports the broader claim about nonviolence.
debates.comment: Changing 'violence' to 'military service' is a meaningful correction that accurately reflects the specific historical account of the saints.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Pancras

debates.before: as early as the fourth century
debates.after: around the turn of the sixth century
debates.concern: The present basilica over Pancras's grave is generally associated with Pope Symmachus and dates to around the late fifth or early sixth century, not as early as the fourth century. The wording also risks implying that the surviving church building itself dates from the fourth century.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Revise the date to reflect the church's traditional association with Pope Symmachus and its late fifth- or early sixth-century construction.
debates.comment: The revision correctly distinguishes the architectural timeline of the basilica, preventing confusion with fourth-century foundations.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Marcellinus & Peter

debates.before: still recited at every celebration of the traditional Eucharistic Prayer
debates.after: still used in celebrations that employ the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer I
debates.concern: The Roman Canon is one of the Church's approved Eucharistic Prayers; it is not recited at every Catholic Mass or at every celebration using a Eucharistic Prayer. The current wording is materially overbroad.
debates.suggestedCorrection: State that Marcellinus and Peter are named in the Roman Canon, also known as Eucharistic Prayer I, while avoiding the claim that it is used at every celebration.
debates.comment: Important liturgical correction; 'traditional Eucharistic Prayer' could be misunderstood as applying to all modern Eucharistic prayers.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Lucy

debates.before: Her father, of Roman origin, died while she was still young, leaving her raised by her mother, Eutychia, whose name suggests Greek ancestry.
debates.after: Her father died while she was still young, leaving her to be raised by her mother, Eutychia.
debates.concern: The traditional account supports the father's early death and Eutychia's role, but the claim that he was of Roman origin and the inference that Eutychia's name establishes Greek ancestry are more specific than the evidence presented and may turn uncertain biographical traditions into historical fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported ethnic inferences or explicitly identify them as traditional or uncertain.
debates.comment: Removing the speculative inferences about ethnic origins strengthens the historical reliability of the biographical note.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Januarius
Proofread articles — St. Catherine of Alexandria

debates.before: the origin of the renowned Monastery of St. Catherine
debates.after: the origin of the monastery's association with St. Catherine
debates.concern: The monastery was built under Justinian centuries before the traditional discovery of Catherine's remains. Calling the discovery the origin of the monastery itself reverses the chronology and may misleadingly suggest that the monastery was founded because of the discovery.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Explain that the traditional discovery gave the already existing monastery its association with St. Catherine, rather than describing it as the monastery's origin.
debates.comment: Important chronological correction preventing the misconception that the monastery was built because of the later discovery of the relics.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Blaise
Proofread articles — Pope St. Sylvester I

debates.before: spanning virtually the entirety of Emperor Constantine's reign
debates.after: spanning much of Emperor Constantine's reign
debates.concern: Sylvester's pontificate lasted from 314 to 335, whereas Constantine's reign began in 306 and ended in 337. It covered much, but not virtually the entirety, of Constantine's reign.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Change the wording to reflect that Sylvester's pontificate covered much of Constantine's reign.
